newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Grain - Malaysia may buy Indian soymeal.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Malaysia may buy Indian soymeal.

text.p: Malaysia could be in the market for between 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes of Indian soymeal for November/December shipment, traders said on Wednesday.

A Singapore-based dealer said there was "strong talk" of Malaysian consumers being in the market for a bulk purchase of 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes of Indian soymeal for November/December shipment at around $310 a tonne C&F.
"We've heard this is being done and that's why the price is being quoted higher," the trader said.
The rumour was, however, disputed by Ho Seng Chan, which usually teams up with three others -- QL Feedstuff , See Hoy Chan and Lam Yong Huat -- to buy soymeal in bulk for Malaysia.

"The four of us went long in early June and are waiting for good prices now," said Johnny Ong, managing director of Ho Seng Chan. "There's a new crop from Argentina in October and we're not in the market now," he added.
Last week, Indian soymeal was indicated at around $295 a tonne C&F Southeast Asia, up about $10 on the previous week.
Indian exporters said on Tuesday that they had so far booked around 100,000 tonnes of soymeal contracts for the 1996/97 (November-October) season.
The Indore-based exporters quoted soymeal at between $261/$262 a tonne FAS (free alongside ship) compared with $188-$189 at the same time last year.

In Malaysia, local dealers quoted imported soymeal in bags unchanged from last week at around 760 ringgit ($305) a tonne ex-factory/godown rates in the central region. Traders in Singapore, however, reported hearing a slightly higher rate of $310 or 773 ringgit.
Domestic soymeal in bags was quoted at last week's level of around 777 ringgit ($312) a tonne.
Thai soymeal prices firmed further to 9.90 baht/kg from 9.70 a week ago as the Thai market waits for Brazilian imports next month, traders said.
They said they expected about 10,000 tonnes of imported soymeal in September.
A trader at Bangkok Produce said a small Thai rainy season soybean crop, being harvest from late August to early October, and earlier limited soybean imports, had reduced local soymeal availability.
He said due to bureaucratic delays in cutting Thai import tariffs, soybean importers had failed to fill about 20,000 tonnes of an import quota by a July 31 deadline set by the Commerce Ministry.
The Thai Soymeal Traders and Importers Association said Thailand imported 23,441 tonnes of soymeal in June against 74,911 tonnes in May and 101,041 tonnes in April.
In other Southeast Asian grain markets, corn continued to ease in Thailad and Indonesia, but held steady in Malaysia.
Thai domestic maize/corn prices paid by feed producers extended a steady decline to an average 4.20 baht/kg this week from 4.28 a week ago on increased supply from the local harvest.
A major feed producer said that the new Thai harvest, mostly from eastern Prachinburi and Chantaburi provinces and some from northeast and north central Thailand, was a major price depressing factor.
The Thai Maize Association said a field survey early this month put the Thai 1996/97 (July/June) maize crop at a projected 4.20 million tonnes against 4.06 million a year ago.
In Indonesia, corn prices were said to be a little lower as supply remained ample in a quiet Jakarta market, traders said.
Corn offers were heard at 500 rupiah/kg in Jakarta and transactions confirmed at 495 rupiah/kg. Forward contracts for September were heard at 490 rupiah, one trader said.
In the main growing area of Lampung in the southern part of Sumatra corn was heard at between 460-80 rupiah/kg.
Shipments of 65,000 tonnes of corn from Argentina and South Africa were due to arrive in Jakarta in early September. Traders said about 90,000 tonnes had been imported in early August.
In Malaysia, bulk corn in the local market was maintained at between 530 and 540 ringgit ($213-$217) ex-factory/godown rates in the central region.
There were no reports of purchases for the expected 100,000 tonnes of corn Malaysia is seen picking up in the next month.
"A" grade wheat in bags was also steady at 880 ringgitt ($353) a tonne ex-factory/godown central region while low-grade wheat was in a range of 580-600 ringgitt ($233-$241).
